The US undersecretary of defence Elbridge Colby has praised Europe for stepping up to take more responsibility for Ukraine’s defence, helping mount the Ukrainian forces mount “a resilient denial defence.”
Colby said Europe and the US “have made tremendous progress in making Nato 3.0 a reality,” while continuing to support Ukraine.
But he said more needs to be done, urging Europe “to focus its defence industrial-based efforts on military efficacy and battlefield utility , rather than ancillary domestic or industrial policy objectives” and continue its spending on Ukraine-related schemes.
“In October, for the second consecutive month, Ukraine gained more territory than Russia and Russian forces suffered their highest monthly casualty toll of the war.”
But in a rather curious part of his statement, Colby appeared to distance the US from some of the recent deep strikes in Russia .
“It is our view that focusing on support, our support on the frontlines and on associated mid-range strikes is the most effective way to enable Ukraine’s defence, and thus to set the conditions for an end to the war. …
While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the frontline.
Moreover, such strikes as especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate. Moreover, it is important to note that the balance of advantage in deep strikes may well favour Moscow.”
“This is not to say that Ukraine should be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back. Rather, that we should be clear about is that the focus of our support should be on enabling and advancing Ukraine’s ability to hold the line of battle and, where possible, make gains.
Strikes focused on the frontline and direct support to that battle area, of course, fall into this category, but consistent with this approach, strikes that target Russia’s war making machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia’s advances on the frontlines.”
Colby also said the US administration “remain firmly committed to bringing this conflict to an end on terms that secure a durable peace,” even as it appears that Russia wants to continue the war.
Germany’s defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that “the fifth war winter … threatens to be harder than the ones before,” as Russia “has further expanded its arsenal of attack drones and ballistic missiles.”
“With daily airstrikes, Russia is trying to take out Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and water supply. It is terrorising Ukraine from the air because it cannot achieve military success on the ground ,” he said.
Pistorius warned that Russia “may intentionally try to cause humanitarian emergencies in Kyiv, Odesa and other large cities to break the Ukrainian people’s resistance.”
“If Russia were to succeed, the consequence would be dramatic, both for Ukraine and for Europe , ” he said.
Earlier, UK’s Wes Streeting said the aim of the meeting is to discuss how to “put Ukraine in the best possible position for future negotiations.”

He said he would give parties one more week before he calls in the party leaders to decide what will happen next, but that he is determined to get to the end of this process soon so that by Christmas, Sweden will either have a new government or can prepare to go back to the polls with a second election.

BBC's Madeline Halpert explains why the US lost its measles elimination status and what it could mean.
After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.
The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. President Donald Trump inspects an honor guard after stepping off Air Force One, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, at Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila, Philippines. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
MANILA, Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing "YMCA" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.
Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.
The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.
The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.
Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
Demonstrators hold signs during a protest against U.S. President Donald Trump's visit to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit and related meetings in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Firdia Linsawati/AP hide caption
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.
"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
"Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.
Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents
A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.
Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence had begun when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from its Palestinian residents.
Dozens of Israeli settlers, some of them armed, moved into eight buildings in al-Duyuk al-Tahta two weeks ago with the backing of the settler organisation Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.
“A vehicle carrying settlers chased him,” Younis said. “There were about 15 settlers in several vehicles. They began firing indiscriminately, killing the woman.”
Witnesses said Palestinian residents began to throw stones to defend themselves, as more settlers arrived at the scene, shooting at civilians and injuring six men.
Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was wounded after he rushed to the scene after learning that his mother had been shot. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters he was in shock when he accidentally collided with a parked car belonging to one of the settlers.
Witnesses said the vehicle was empty at the time, but that settlers responded by opening fire, wounding Arafat in the torso.
Naama Fidhat said her husband was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah when Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him. She said Israeli soldiers also arrested their son, Wadha’s grandson, early the following morning.
“What did we do? We didn’t do anything,” she said. “This is our house, they were the ones who came with weapons … we were unarmed, we were sleeping.”
The Israeli military said a group of Palestinians in ​a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”. It said the Palestinians exited the vehicle and attacked the Israelis, who opened fire at the Palestinians. “There are Israeli and Palestinian ​casualties in the incident,” the military said.
The arrival of the Israeli settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta had raised fears among Palestinian residents who have faced repeated attacks in the area.
The Binyamin regional council, which covers 47 illegal settlements, claimed the properties in the village had been bought from Palestinians, but Jericho’s governor, Hussein Hamayel, disputed the claim, saying the land belonged to the state and could not legally be sold.
Human rights activists said settlers had assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg during the takeover earlier this month.
“Since the settlers moved into the area on 4 November our lives have been turned upside down,” Younis told the Guardian. “We used to live peacefully and safely on our farms, but since the settlers arrived, our lives have become a living hell. I own 53 dunams [5.3 hectares] of farmland with greenhouses, but we are no longer allowed to access them. We have suffered devastating financial losses, and now people are being killed as well.”
There has been a sharp ​rise in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 six-day war. UN bodies and most ​countries deem the settlements illegal, which Israel disputes.
On Tuesday, Suleiman Abu Srour, a photographer for the Palestinian news agency Wafa, was beaten by Israeli soldiers while covering events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta . Wafa said he suffered fractures and bruises, was detained for six hours and had his phone confiscated before being released.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in “illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians” in the West Bank .
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”
Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on a Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers .
Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.
Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions.
“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions.
“We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action, but provided no detail.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past.
“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.

A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.
There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.
According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.
There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.
They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.
Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Palestinian children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.
Fadda's daughter-in-law, Nema al-Fahidat, told the BBC that she died from a single bullet wound to the head. "It destroyed her brain," she said.
According to the Palestinian accounts, Fadda's son, Arafat, rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said, injuring several Palestinians, including Arafat.
"My husband, when he saw his mother, was not paying attention. He crashed into the vehicle. The vehicle was empty," Nema said.
"My husband got out of his car and tried to reach his mother and the injured young men. Then he was shot."
She added: "We tried to gather the injured people and move them away from the settler. We brought them here. But he kept firing, firing, firing. Even after we had brought the wounded young men here and moved them away from him, he continued shooting."
Nema said young Palestinians threw stones at the settlers after seeing what happened, but asked: "What can stones do against bullets?"
Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday
The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".
Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."
Later, an Israeli military source said Fadda was shot by an Israeli civilian and that there was no evidence that she had been involved in the confrontation near her home.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Israel's police force said it had opened an investigation, and that officers and forensic technicians had been collecting evidence and interviewing witnesses.
The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.

A BBC team saw settlers at the end of the street where Fadda was shot on Tuesday, as well as Israeli flags flying from four of the houses that they had moved into earlier this month.
A group of settlers set up a new outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo)
In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.

Carney eyes 'other options' for embattled Canadian auto sector on China trip
Canada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests for Ottawa as it grapples with US tariffs on the sector.
Now Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he is looking to China, where he is on a visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit (Apec), as part of the solution.
But that avenue is not without controversy, and is once again drawing the ire of those close to Donald Trump.
While in Cambodia earlier this week, Carney told reporters that Canada could turn to European and Asian carmakers to save its auto manufacturing sector if a trade deal with the US could not be reached.
If Canadian auto workers are "not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.
He went on to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Tuesday for their second head-to-head in less than a year. The two talked of the importance of developing their relations, and Carney said they had agreed to further tariff cuts.
Neither side mentioned vehicles specifically, though analysts suggest the issue will have been prominent in their minds.
Carney and Xi met on Tuesday to discuss cooperation and trade ahead of this week's Apec summit
In January, Carney said that opening the door to China's electric vehicles , external (EVs) could result in investment into Canadian-owned companies and the creation of manufacturing jobs in the sector.
American tariffs on imports of Canadian-made vehicles have led to thousands of job losses in Canada and anxiety over the future, as 90% of cars made in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US.
At the same time, China has been eyeing Canada as a potential entry-point to the North American EV market. Earlier this year, Canada announced that it would let in 49,000 EVs from China at a low tariff rate, with plans to raise that quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030.
The move was a significant break from the US, which tariffs Chinese EVs heavily to protect domestic manufacturing.
Peter Navarro, Trump's senior counsel for trade and manufacturing, warned the prime minister against cosying up to China in a post on X , external .
"Are u really threatening to play China off the US? This is offensive in the extreme," he wrote on Monday. "You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive."
His comments were reposted by Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada.
Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu toured a Chinese EV plant earlier this month
Chinese EV manufacturers like BYD and Chery have already been lobbying the Canadian government for market access.
Last week, Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China , external . He told reporters afterwards that Canadians could expect to see affordable Chinese EVs in Canada by early 2027.
These moves come as the toll of US tariffs on Canada's auto sector has become harder to ignore.
Stellantis, a multinational car manufacturer that made models like the Dodge Challenger in Canada, recently announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario.
The facility had been idle since 2023 for a planned retooling, but what was supposed to be a temporary shutdown became permanent after Trump's tariffs.
The sale has led to speculation that a Chinese EV manufacturer could move into the facility, after Canadian media outlet CTV News reported , external , citing anonymous sources, that Stellantis was planning to lease back 25% of its plant to assemble "affordable" EVs.
The idea is unpopular with Ontario Premier Doug Ford. In a letter to Carney, he warned against opening the door for Chinese EV kits to be assembled at the Brampton plant.
China overwhelmingly builds its cars at home and ships them whole - or to be assembled in kits - overseas.
Canada's deal with China signals it is serious about shift from US
Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, said introducing Chinese auto manufacturing in Canada would be "controversial" due to fears that Canadian jobs could be lost and that the North American industry could be eroded.
"We want to make sure they're hiring Canadian workers, that they are helping train Canadian workers and that they are transferring the technology over," Ong said.
Carney noted there are "clear guardrails" in how Canada deals with China, including barring work on sensitive matters like artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Canada has also eyed other partnerships. It is notably pursuing associate member status with the EU, and had signed a free trade deal with the Philippines earlier this week.
Just how much Canada is willing to embrace Chinese manufacturing, however, still depends on the outcome of ongoing US-Canada trade talks.
Progress has been made in negotiations, Carney recently said, but differences remain. It is unclear if Trump and Carney will speak on the sidelines of the Apec summit later this week.

A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.

China said on Tuesday it has "no information" on whether US President Donald Trump would meet Kim Jong-un, after the US president left open the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader on his Asia trip.
"I have no information regarding this matter," foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a news briefing in Beijing, a day before Trump was expected in Shenzhen for an APEC meeting.
Before departing for China, Trump, who met Kim three times during his first term, left open the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader.
"We may meet with Kim Jong-un also, so that'll be good," Trump told reporters, adding that whether Kim would make the trip was "up to President Xi" of China.
As Trump made the remarks, North Korean state media reported that Kim and his family, accompanied by party officials, travelled to a tourist zone near the northern border with China on Sunday and Monday.
Photos released by the official Korean Central News Agency show Kim sitting on an armchair, grinning, with a cigarette in his hand and sunglasses on, at what appeared to be a ski resort, with his wife Ri Sol Ju standing behind him.
Another photo shows his young daughter Ju Ae, whom Seoul's spy agency has said is being groomed to be Kim's successor, skiing downhill in a white outfit but without a helmet.
The city of Samjiyon is located near the Chinese border and is close to Mount Paektu, considered by North Koreans to be the sacred birthplace of Kim's father, Jong-il.
As he toured the resort, including ski centres and hotels, Kim "expressed great satisfaction, saying that all the structures are really impeccable as they were built in a delicate way", KCNA reported.
"The more he looked at it, the more admiration he felt at the spectacular scenery reminiscent of a town in the forest," it said.
While Kim made the visit near China, which is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, experts say it was unlikely intended to signal plans to travel to the summit.
The straight-line distance between the two cities is more than 2,500 kilometres (1,553 miles).
"The KCNA report does not contain any message aimed at the United States and there are no signs of preparations for a meeting," Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, told the AFP news agency.
"Kim's visit therefore is hard to be seen as a preparation for any North Korea-US meeting this week," he said.
Trump and Kim met in Singapore in June 2018, then in Hanoi in February 2019 and at the Demilitarised Zone in North Korea in June 2019.
The meetings came after Trump initially mocked Kim as "rocket man" during a speech in 2017.
The US president said in August that he expected to meet later this year with Kim, hoping to revive the bond he claims to have forged with the leader of nuclear-armed North Korea in his first term.

China offers tariff cuts on Canadian pork and seafood, as Canada extends exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminium.
Canada and China have agreed to cut tariffs on more goods, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney continues to look to decrease his country’s dependence on the United States amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
Meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday, Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced new tariff remissions, building on an agreement they made in January to open up trade and start to repair a strained diplomatic relationship.
China will offer tariff relief on about 400 million Canadian dollars ($280m) worth of Canadian exports, including frozen pork and seafood, said a statement from Carney’s office.
Canada, in exchange, will keep tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products in place for another two years, and add remissions to another 32 steel and aluminium items that Canada doesn’t have enough of.
Xi said stronger ties served both countries’ interests and supported global stability and prosperity.
Carney praised the greater predictability in the relationship and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50 percent by the end of the decade.
Under the January agreement, Canada lowered its 100 percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 percent, allowing an initial 49,000 vehicles into the country each year. That cap is set to rise to 70,000 over five years.
In return, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products and recently extended relief for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab for another two years.
The deal comes a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Washington fail to hold together the closely integrated North American auto industry.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia on Monday. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”
The comments prompted a backlash from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro, who responded by asking whether Carney was threatening to “play China off the US”.
“This is offensive in the extreme,” he said, adding that Carney should be more worried that China would “eat Canada alive”.
Carney has made looking to markets beyond the US a central part of his economic strategy, as Trump’s tariffs hit Canadian industries, including auto manufacturing, as well as steel and aluminium.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down in August , but Carney said on Saturday that he’d spoken with Trump and senior officials, and that while differences remained, there was progress towards a possible deal.
He also met with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday, with both countries reaffirming their commitment to renew the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement , according to Carney’s office.
One year after Carney visited Mexico, during which they launched a strategic partnership, the two leaders agreed to keep expanding bilateral trade and investment. They also highlighted a 19-percent increase in merchandise trade in the first nine months of this year, compared with the same period last year.

The Israeli parliament on Tuesday elected as new speaker an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace current Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Matan Kahana, a former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of the agenda of Netanyahu.
The Israeli parliament, or Knesset , elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Sixty six lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate, who received 52 votes.
The parliament speaker is an important office given that it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
Read more Eisenkot pushes October 7 inquiry as Netanyahu targets Arab parties in tense new parliament
Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of the agenda of Netanyahu, Israel 's longest serving prime minister who has been in and out of office for three decades.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a majority in the 120-member Knesset in October 27 elections , with the two blocs trading barbs since then.
The vote for parliament speaker crystallised their standoff, with a heated debate before the vote.
In October, Eisenkot's wide-ranging bloc secured 48 seats, while Netanyahu's finished with 53. Two Arab-majority slates won an unprecedented 19 seats on the back of anger over Netanyahu's hard-right government.
On Tuesday, the two lists voted for Eisenkot's candidate Kahana as parliament speaker, with one Arab Knesset member absent.
"I will be a Knesset speaker for everyone, irrespective of race, religion or gender," said Kahana during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.
Netanyahu's and Eisenkot's parties met Sunday on the possibility of joining a unity government but the meeting appeared to be largely a formality, with both men saying they should be prime minister.
Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume war on Iran , has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government.
Eisenkot said afterwards that Netanyahu was unfit to "remain at the helm of government for even one more minute" after an explosive media report that his allies tried to make up allegations of fraud to frame lawmakers from the Arab minority.
On Tuesday, Israel's central elections committee released a statement regarding the ongoing investigation into the fraud accusations led by the Shin Bet intelligence agency.
"At this stage, there is no evidence that bribes were paid to voters on a scale that could have affected the election results," it said.
With Kahana at the helm and if Eisenkot retains the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, he has an opportunity to deal serious blows to Netanyahu's legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
Eisenkot has said he wants to rescind sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
The judicial reforms initiated shortly after Netanyahu began his latest term in December 2022 triggered some of Israel's largest ever protests, bringing tens of thousands to the streets, with liberals fearing an erosion of the country's democracy.
Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas 's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel's security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.
Kahana, who is now a member of Eisenkot's Yashar party, served in a short-lived non-Netanyahu government in 2021 and 2022 as minister for religious services in which he clashed with ultra-Orthodox Jews by seeking to reduce the power of the Chief Rabbinate.
Kahana himself is an observant Jew, part of Eisenkot's efforts to form a broad coalition that ranges from secular liberals to religious conservatives.
As parliament speaker, Kahana succeeds Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally who has held the position since 2022.
The parliament speaker serves as acting head of state when the president is unable to perform his duties.

A woman holds an Iranian flag as part of a pro-government campaign beneath a billboard depicting a launched missile, a man with a rifle, people and current and the late Revolutionary Guard missile force commanders with clenched fists, with a sign which reads in Farsi: "The sky is a place for our pride and loyalty," in downtown Tehran, Iran, Monday. Vahid Salemi/AP hide caption
CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.
The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.
Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.
A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.
The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
This is a locator map for the Gulf Cooperation Council member states: Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and United Arab Emirates. AP hide caption
Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.
Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.
"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."
With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.
Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.
"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."
Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

Appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of Netanyahu’s outgoing government
The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu .
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot , the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu . Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.
The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition. As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda. They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.
Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.
Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.
Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances. “It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed. Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.

61 yaşındaki Karakaş, geçtiğimiz aylarda estetisyen Müge Zopun ile tanıştı. Karakaş, tanıştıktan 15 gün sonra kalp krizi geçirdi. Yoğun bakımda tedavi gören Karakaş, zorlu sürecin ardından yeniden sağlığına kavuştu. Karakaş, "Ben Dilber'in acısını Müge ile yendim. Bu ağır krizde de Müge her zaman yanımdaydı" dedi.
Müge Zopun ise "Dilber Hanım’ı çok severdim, çok saygı duyardım. Vefatına da çok üzüldüm. Allah rahmet eylesin, keşke yaşasaydı. Ben ona gerçekten büyük saygı duyuyorum. İbrahim’in her zaman arkasındayım. Birbirimize ömrümüzün sonuna kadar her şekilde varız. O bana, ben ona destek oldum" diye konuştu.
Geçtiğimiz günlerde birlikteliklerinde kriz yaşayan Karakaş ve Zopun canlı yayında nişanlandı.
Çift, takılan yüzükler sonrasında Dilber Ay'ın "Tavukları Pişirmişem" şarkısıyla eğlendi. Karakaş ve Zopun tepki çekti.
"YAĞLI KAPI BULDUN" Dilber Ay'ın kızı Filiz Çelik, Karakaş'a sert tepki göstererek, "Sen acı yaşamadın. 3 ay sonra arabayı sattın, klip çektin. Müge hanımı sorduğumda, 'Herhangi birisi' dedin bana. Sen 7 yıl 4 aydır evlisin. Sen zaten çalışmayı sevmeyen birisin. Bir yağlı kapı daha buldun" ifadelerini kullanmıştı.

63 yaşında hayatını kaybeden Dilber Ay, İbrahim Karakaş'a ilk görüşte aşık olduğunu açıklamıştı.
"Hacı Ağa", "Zorunda mıyım?", "Gelmezsen gelme" gibi eserlerle tanınan Dilber Ay , 2019 yılında geçirdiği kalp krizi sonrası hayatını kaybetti. Eşinin vefatı sonrası uzun süre yas tuttuğunu söyleyen İbrahim Karakaş şimdilerde ikinci baharını yaşıyor.
Karakaş, 2021 yılında tanıştığı ve bir buçuk yıl sonra aşk yaşamaya başladığı Müge Zopun ile evlilik yoluna girdi. Geçtiğimiz aylarda Dilber Ay'ın çocuklarıyla yaşadığı tartışmayla gündem olan İbrahim Karakaş , Star TV ekranlarında evlilik yolunda ilk adımı attı.
İbrahim Karakaş ile Müge Zopun, Songül Karlı ve Uğur Arslan'ın sunduğu “Songül ve Uğur ile Sana Değer” programının bugünkü canlı yayınında nişanlandı.
Çiftin yüzüklerini şarkıcı Güler Işık taktı. Davul zurna eşliğinde stüdyoda nişanlanan çiftin Dilber Ay'ın "Tavukları Pişirmişem" şarkısıyla eğlenmesi de dikkatlerden kaçmadı.
İbrahim Karakaş, Dilber Ay'ın vefatı sonrası kızlarıyla bir bağı kalmadığını ve iletişime geçmediklerini söyledi.
Canlı yayına telefonla bağlanan Dilber Ay'ın kızı Satı Hanım ise İbrahim Karakaş ile Müge Zopun'a mutluluklar diledi. Dilber Ay'ın kızı "İbrahim Bey bize babalık yaptı, üvey babamın nişanlanması zoruma gitti" dedi.

texts.https://www.dw.com/en/apec-summit-what-t:
Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
The leaders of China , the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.
Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.
Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."
Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.
"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.
"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."
Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.
Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.
She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.
Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."
She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.
With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.
Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.

Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine .
"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."
Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.
"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.
Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.
An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."
The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.
He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."
He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.
"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.
"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."
W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran .
The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."
Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.
"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

Ünlü oyuncu Ezgi Mola, Mustafa Aksakallı ile evliliğini sonlandırmasının ardından özel hayatında yeni bir sayfa açtı. Yaklaşık bir buçuk yıl önce boşanan Mola, yeni sevgilisi olduğu belirtilen Yaşar Çağlak ile ilk kez birlikte görüntülendi.

Haziran 2025'te tek celsede boşanan ikili, ayrılık kararını birlikte aldıklarını ve dostluklarını sürdüreceklerini açıklamıştı.

Kanal D ’nin reyting rekortmeni Uzak Şehir , 16 Kasım Pazartesi akşamı yayınlanan yeni bölümüyle üç listede de zirvede kaldı ama geçen hafta gördüğü çift haneyi koruyamadı. TOTAL’de 10,10'dan 9,79'a inen dizinin düşüşünü bir reyting uzmanı X’te ara tatile bağladı. Uzman, geçen sezon ara tatile denk gelen 37. bölümde de benzer bir düşüş yaşandığını ve dizinin sonraki hafta 1,56 puan yükseldiğini hatırlattı.
Uzak Şehir , 16 Kasım Pazartesi akşamı ekrana gelen yeni bölümüyle TOTAL, AB ve ABC1'de yine ilk sırada yer aldı. Uzak Şehir, 9 Kasım'da 10,10 alarak yeni sezonda yalnızca iki dizinin görebildiği çift haneye ulaşan üçüncü yapım olmuştu. Ancak dizi , bir hafta önce yakaladığı çift haneli reytingi koruyamadı. TOTAL'de 10,10'dan 9,79'a inen dizi, AB'de 7,50'den 6,80'e, ABC1'de ise 9,25'ten 8,08'e geriledi.
En sert kayıp ABC1'de yaşandı. Dizi bu listede tek haftada 1,17 puan kaybetti. Üstelik düşüş yalnızca Uzak Şehir'e özgü değildi. Aynı akşam ATV 'de yayınlanan rakibi Altı Üstü İstanbul da TOTAL'de 7,43'ten 7,08'e indi. Düşüşe rağmen rakibiyle arasındaki fark açık kaldı. Uzak Şehir, akşamı Altı Üstü İstanbul'un TOTAL'de 2,71, AB'de 2,56, ABC1'de ise 1,67 puan önünde tamamladı.
Böylece Uzak Şehir, pazartesi akşamının en çok izlenen yapımı olma unvanını bu hafta da kimseye kaptırmadı.
Dizinin reytingindeki gerilemenin ardından bir reyting uzmanı X hesabından yaptığı paylaşımla konuya açıklık getirdi.
Uzmana göre bu tablonun nedeni bölümün kendisi değil, ara tatil haftasıydı. Paylaşımda, saat 23.00'e kadar toplam televizyon izleme oranının (TTV) ortalamada 2,5 puan düşük seyrettiği belirtildi. Ara tatil dönemlerinde seyahatler ve değişen akşam alışkanlıkları, televizyon izleme oranlarını genellikle aşağı çeker. Yani ekran başındaki toplam izleyici sayısı azaldığı için pazartesi akşamının iki lider dizisi de puan kaybetti. Uzman, 'Haftaya burası dengeye gelir' diyerek düşüşün kalıcı olmadığının altını çizdi.
Uzman, yorumunu dizinin geçen sezonki performansıyla destekledi.
Paylaşıma göre Uzak Şehir , geçen yıl ara tatilin öncesindeki ve sonrasındaki bölümlerde 1,5 puanlık artışlar yakalamıştı. Ara tatile denk gelen 37. bölüm ise güçlü bir bölüm olmasına rağmen düşüş yaşamıştı.
Peki sonra ne oldu? Dizi bir sonraki hafta 1,56 puanlık artışla yeniden yükselişe geçmişti.
Uzmanın yorumuna göre bu sezon da benzer bir tablo bekleniyor. Gelecek pazartesi yayınlanacak yeni bölüm, Uzak Şehir'in yeniden çift haneye dönüp dönmeyeceğini gösterecek.

Manuela Perteghella had criticised plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham amid growing opposition to the proposal.
The university said it would spend the next six months working with partners including the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust to explore the institute's future in Stratford.
The decision comes after criticism from Stratford-upon-Avon MP Manuela Perteghella and a petition that attracted more than 12,000 signatures.
The move from its home at Mason Croft had been due to take place in September.
The postgraduate research institute announced on Friday that it had been told it would leave Stratford and relocate to the University of Birmingham's Edgbaston campus, with future plans unclear for its Mason Croft base, historic gardens and playing fields.
Announcing the pause on Tuesday evening, University of Birmingham vice-chancellor and principal Prof Adam Tickell said he had heard "very clearly" how much the institute mattered to Stratford-upon-Avon and the wider Shakespeare community.
"I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the Institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon," he said.
The planned move from Mason Croft has been paused while the university explores future options
The university said it would work with the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, institute staff, students, alumni and other partners over the coming months.
Tickell said the university's commitment to Shakespearean studies had "never been in doubt" but added that interest in studying in Stratford had remained low for several years.
He said related subjects had seen significant growth on the university's Birmingham campus, while the city's creative industries sector offered opportunities for Shakespearean research and scholarship.
"Over the next six months, we will work with the Shakespeare Institute, the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and other partners, students, and alumni to ensure that the Shakespeare Institute re-establishes itself at the heart of scholarship, performance and reception for England's greatest poet in both Birmingham and Stratford-upon-Avon," he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, Liberal Democrat MP Perteghella described the proposed move as "ill-thought" and "shocking".
She said she would raise the issue in Parliament and write to the university about her "deep disappointment" and concerns for the institute's future.
The University of Birmingham said it would spend the next six months exploring the centre's future
The MP backed a petition launched by the Stratford Herald calling on the university to keep the institute in Stratford-upon-Avon.
Actors Samuel West and Dame Janet Suzman have also backed the campaign.
The Shakespeare Institute, which celebrated its 75th anniversary in July, was founded at Mason Croft in 1951 and has worked with academics, writers and performers including Dame Judi Dench.

ABD ’li teknoloji devi Apple, bazı iPhone modellerinin yetkili servisler dışında onarılmasını engelleyerek planlı eskitme uyguladığı iddiasıyla Fransa ’da hakim karşısına çıkacak. Paris’te görülecek dava , ülkede onarımı engelleme suçlamasıyla bir telefon üreticisine karşı açılan ilk dava olacak.
Dosyaya yakın kaynakların aktardığına göre Apple Inc. ile Apple Distribution International, 17 Haziran 2027'den itibaren dört gün sürecek duruşmalarda yargılanacak. Şirkete, Kasım 2021 ile Temmuz 2024 arasında bazı iPhone modellerinin yetkili servisler dışında onarılmasını ve yenilenmesini engellediği gerekçesiyle “onarımı ve yenilemeyi engelleme” suçlaması yöneltiliyor.
Apple ise “Bu asılsız iddialara kesinlikle itiraz ediyoruz” açıklamasını yaptı.
İddiaya göre telefonların işletim sistemi, parçaların seri numarasını kontrol ediyor. Parça yetkili servis dışında değiştirildiğinde bazı özellikler devre dışı kalıyordu. Örneğin bazı modellerde ön kamera değiştirildiğinde yüz tanıma (Face ID) çalışmıyor, pilin sağlık durumu bilgisi de etkilenebiliyordu. Bu yöntem, Apple logosu taşımayan yedek parçaların kullanılmasını da imkânsız hâle getiriyordu.
Davaya konu olan modeller arasında iPhone XS’ten iPhone 15 Pro Max’e kadar uzanan seriler, iPhone 12, 13 ve 14 serileri ile 2020 ve 2022 model iPhone SE yer alıyor.
Fransız derneği “Halte à l’Obsolescence Programmée” (HOP), 7 Aralık 2022'de Apple hakkında suç duyurusunda bulunmuştu. Dernek, dava kararının dört yıllık soruşturmanın ardından geldiğini belirtti.
Apple, Fransa ’da daha önce de iPhone ’larla ilgili bir soruşturmayla karşılaşmıştı. Şirket, Şubat 2020'de yanıltıcı ticari uygulamalar nedeniyle başlatılan kovuşturmayı sona erdirmek için 25 milyon avro para cezası ödemeyi kabul etmişti.
Planlı eskitme, üreticilerin ürünlerinin kullanım ömrünü kasıtlı olarak kısaltması anlamına geliyor. Fransa ’da 2021'den bu yana bir üreticinin cihazlarının onarılmasını engellemesi de planlı eskitmeyle bağlantılı ayrı bir suç sayılıyor.
Bu suçlar için 2 yıla kadar hapis ve 300 bin avro para cezası öngörülüyor. Para cezası, elde edilen kazançla orantılı olarak şirketin yıllık ortalama cirosunun yüzde 5'ine kadar çıkabiliyor.
texts.https://tr.euronews.com/2026/11/17/apple:
Apple, bazı iPhone modellerinin yetkili servisler dışındaki tamirini engelleyerek planlı eskitme uyguladığı iddiasıyla önümüzdeki yıl haziran ayında Paris'te yargılanacak.
ABD'li teknoloji devi hakkında Fransız savcılar tarafından açılan dava, “tamir ve yenilemeyi engelleme” suçlamasına dayanıyor. Planlı Eskitmeye Karşı Mücadele Derneği (Stop Planned Obsolescence), Aralık 2022'de yaptığı şikâyetin ardından gelen bu gelişmeyi bir ilk olarak nitelendirerek memnuniyetle karşıladı.
Apple ise AFP'ye yaptığı açıklamada, “Bu temelsiz iddiaları kesinlikle reddediyoruz,” dedi.
Planlı eskitme, üreticilerin ürünlerinin kullanım ömrünü kasıtlı olarak kısaltmak için başvurduğu yöntemleri ifade ediyor. Genellikle elektronik cihazlarda görülen bu uygulamalar, tüketicileri ürünlerini daha sık yenilemeye yöneltiyor.
Suçlu bulunması halinde Apple, 300 bin euroya kadar para cezasının yanı sıra yıllık gelirinin yüzde 5'ine kadar ek para cezası ödeyebilir. Bu tutar, haberin yayımlandığı tarih itibarıyla yaklaşık 21,7 milyar euroya karşılık geliyor. Şirket ayrıca müşterilerin tazminat talepleriyle de karşılaşabilir.
AFP'ye konuşan davaya yakın bir kaynağa göre, Apple Distribution International ve ana şirketi Apple Inc, 17 Haziran'da başlayacak dört günlük duruşmada yargılanacak.
Şirketler, Kasım 2021 ile Temmuz 2024 arasındaki iki buçuk yılı aşkın dönemde çeşitli iPhone modellerinin tamir edilmesini engellemekle suçlanıyor.
Söz konusu modeller arasında iPhone XS'in yanı sıra iPhone 12, 13, 14 ve 15 serileri ile 2022'de piyasaya sürülen iPhone SE de bulunuyor.
Kaynak, Apple'ın yazılımını, telefonların yetkili servis ağı dışındaki işletmelerde tamir edilmesini veya yenilenmesini “imkânsız hale getirecek” şekilde yapılandırmakla suçlandığını belirtti.
Örneğin, kamera yetkisiz bir tamir servisi tarafından değiştirildiğinde Face ID yüz tanıma özelliği devre dışı kalabiliyor ya da “pil sağlığı” göstergesi çalışmayı durdurabiliyor.
İddialara göre amaç, Apple'ın amiral gemisi ürününün satışlarını ve çok uluslu şirketin gelirini artırmaktı. Şirketin yıllık geliri 400 milyar doları aşarken, bu gelirin yaklaşık yarısı iPhone satışlarından elde ediliyor.
Stop Planned Obsolescence derneğinin Apple hakkında açtığı ilk dava bu değil.
Şirket, Şubat 2021'de eski iPhone modellerini yavaşlatabilecek yazılım güncellemeleri hakkında kullanıcıları bilgilendirmediği gerekçesiyle 25 milyon euro ödemeyi kabul etmişti.
Bu uzlaşma, Apple'ın Aralık 2017'de, pil ömrü azalan eski telefonların performansını yeni iOS yazılımıyla yavaşlattığını kabul etmesinin ardından dünya genelinde karşılaştığı davalardan biriydi.

Actress Gabrielle Creevy stars as Liz Rich, bringing "absolute authenticity to the role"
The "real-life ghost story" of a family who experienced "frightening, inexplicable" things after moving to the countryside has been turned into a new TV drama.
The Witch Farm tells the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich who left London with their son Jonathan for a remote farmhouse in the foothills of the Brecon Beacons, determined to make a fresh start.
At first the isolation felt like freedom, but the family claimed things began to happen around the house leading them to feel increasingly scared.
Writer and creator, Danny Robins, met Liz who told him "her incredible story", becoming a four part series he beleives will "really surprise people".
Danny Robins hopes that new TV drama will raise the question, do ghosts exist?
Robins, who was also the executive producer of the project, explained how the idea for the four-part series came from a podcast he made for the BBC called The Battersea Poltergeist , which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story".
"It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.
In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.
They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.
Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm .
"Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.
After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.
The Witch Farm is based on the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich
Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it.
"It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."
He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.
Robins also hopes to raise the question – 'do ghosts exist?', sparking the debate between belief and scepticism.
"What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.
The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy.
She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."
Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."
Creevy recently featured in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.
Robins said The Witch Farm is "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.
He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in it's creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."
The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from Sunday, 22 November.

Vice-chancellor halts proposed relocation from Stratford-upon-Avon but offers no guarantees over future
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move its much-loved Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to its city campus after an outcry from scholars, actors and enthusiasts around the world.
Prof Adam Tickell, the university’s vice-chancellor and principal, issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying proposals to relocate the institute and its renowned 60,000-volume library to the university’s Edgbaston campus would be put on hold while its future was explored.
“Over the past few days, we have heard very clearly how much the Shakespeare Institute matters not only to the University of Birmingham but also to Stratford-upon-Avon, to our partners at the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and to people who love Shakespeare around the world,” Tickell said.
“I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon.” He pointed out that interest in studying in Shakespeare’s home town had been low in recent years and made no promises about the institute’s future.
Prof Michael Dobson, the director of the Shakespeare Institute, who said he would resign if the move went ahead, described the announcement as “a start”, but said he would have preferred the decision to be reversed rather than paused.
The original decision to relocate, announced to devastated institute staff and students last week, was lambasted on social media as “near-philistine”, “unbelievably stupid”, “extraordinarily sad and shortsighted” and “an appalling act of cultural vandalism”.
A petition protesting against the move, led by the actors Samuel West and Dame Janet Suzman, rapidly gathered 15,000 signatures, as supporters of the institute around the world registered their anger at the proposal.
West said the campaign would continue. “The university’s statement is a masterpiece of Shakespearean equivocation and mild threat but we must be thankful that they have seen sense and the immediate danger is past.
“It feels like they still don’t get the idea that specialised excellence in a unique place needn’t always be a matter of numbers; their bottom line is always the bottom line.
“In any case, a wonderful 48 hours of love and publicity for the Institute, if a hellish one for its students and staff. The campaign continues to collect signatures.”
Tickell said: “The university’s commitment to Shakespearean studies has never been in doubt but we need to be honest about the challenges and opportunities the institute faces.
“Interest in studying in Stratford has remained very low for several years. At the same time, we have seen significant growth for related subjects on our Birmingham campus and the thriving creative industries sector in Birmingham creates real opportunities for Shakespearean research and scholarship.
“Over the next six months, we will work with the Shakespeare Institute, the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and other partners, students and alumni to ensure that the Shakespeare Institute re-establishes itself at the heart of scholarship, performance and reception for England’s greatest poet in both Birmingham and Stratford-upon-Avon.”
Dobson said: “I look forward to continuing to try to persuade the university management that we can find a viable, permanent future for the institute in Stratford-upon-Avon.”
